Rewrite the whole page correctly and discard the original page
Draw a single line through the error, initial, date, and write the correction

explanation: Legal medical records require transparent corrections: single line, initials/date, no obliteration.

distractorExplanations.a: A correction must be initialed and dated so the author and timing are traceable; an unsigned change is not acceptable.
distractorExplanations.b: Blacking out obliterates the original entry; it must stay legible under a single line to avoid suspicion of tampering.
distractorExplanations.c: Discarding the original page destroys part of the legal record, which is treated as tampering.

prompt: Prior authorization is typically required when:

options.text: A payer requires approval before covering certain services or medications
A patient is seen by an out-of-network provider for a covered emergency
A patient on a PPO plan books a visit with an in-network specialist
A patient requests copies of their records from the practice

explanation: Prior auth is payer approval before selected services/drugs are covered.

distractorExplanations.b: Federal rules bar plans from requiring prior authorization for emergency services, including out-of-network ER care.
distractorExplanations.c: PPO plans generally allow in-network specialist visits without a referral or prior authorization; that is an HMO rule.
distractorExplanations.d: A records request falls under the HIPAA right of access, which involves no payer approval at all.

prompt: Which statement about referral management is correct?

options.text: PPO plans generally require a PCP referral before any specialist visit
A referral approved once covers unlimited specialist visits for the year
Many HMO plans require referrals/authorizations before specialty care
Original Medicare Part B requires a PCP referral for every specialist visit

prompt: HIPAA's Privacy Rule primarily protects

Employment records held by a covered entity as employer
Education records covered by FERPA
Protected health information (PHI)

prompt: Informed consent requires that the patient

options.text: Sign the form after the MA explains the surgical risks
Be told risks, benefits, and alternatives and agree voluntarily
Be told the risks and benefits, without discussing alternatives
Be told risks and benefits after the procedure has been completed

explanation: Informed consent is voluntary agreement after adequate disclosure and opportunity for questions. Information must be given in understandable terms.

distractorExplanations.a: Disclosing procedure risks is the provider's duty; the MA may witness the signature but cannot obtain informed consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Alternatives, including no treatment, are a required element of informed consent, not an optional extra.
distractorExplanations.d: Consent must be obtained before the procedure; disclosure afterward cannot make the treatment consented.

prompt: Which situation is reportable as suspected child abuse in most U.S. jurisdictions for mandated reporters?

options.text: A toddler with scattered bruises over the shins and knees from active play
A child with unexplained patterned bruises and inconsistent history
A child whose parent declines a flu vaccine after counseling
A child who misses one appointment with no other concerns noted

explanation: Mandated reporters must report reasonable suspicion of abuse/neglect; patterned injuries with inconsistent history are classic red flags.

distractorExplanations.a: Bruises over bony prominences like shins and knees in active toddlers are typical accidental injuries, not a red flag.
distractorExplanations.c: Declining one vaccine after counseling is a parental decision and not, by itself, reasonable suspicion of neglect.
distractorExplanations.d: A single missed appointment without other concerns does not meet the reasonable-suspicion threshold for reporting.

prompt: Which best describes 'negligence' in a healthcare malpractice context?

options.text: Failure to meet the standard of care with no resulting harm
Failure to meet the standard of care causing harm
Intentional touching of a patient without consent
An unexpected poor outcome despite proper care

explanation: Negligence is breach of duty (standard of care) that proximately causes damages.

distractorExplanations.a: Negligence requires all four Ds; a breach without damages (harm) does not support a malpractice claim.
distractorExplanations.c: Intentional unconsented touching is battery, an intentional tort, rather than negligence.
distractorExplanations.d: A poor outcome when the standard of care was met is not negligence; there is no breach of duty.

prompt: A living will typically

options.text: Names a healthcare proxy to make medical decisions
States wishes about life-sustaining treatment
Is a physician order to withhold CPR in any setting
Directs how the patient's property is distributed

explanation: Living wills document preferences for end-of-life/life-sustaining care when the patient lacks capacity. It applies when the patient cannot communicate.

distractorExplanations.a: Naming a proxy is done in a durable power of attorney for health care, a separate advance directive.
distractorExplanations.c: A DNR or POLST is a medical order signed by a clinician; a living will is the patient's own statement of wishes.
distractorExplanations.d: Distribution of property is handled by a last will and testament, not by a living will.

Limited to licensed lab scientists under a lab director's review

prompt: Which is an example of battery in clinical care?

options.text: Threatening a patient with an injection so they comply
Performing a procedure after valid informed consent
Touching or treating a patient without consent
Sharing a patient's diagnosis with a coworker not involved in care

Hand hygiene can be skipped if gloves were worn throughout
Blood and certain body fluids of all patients may be infectious
Sweat and intact skin are handled as potentially infectious material

prompt: A 'Good Samaritan' statute typically protects

options.text: Emergency aid given by an on-duty clinician during a scheduled clinic shift
Grossly negligent emergency aid given at a roadside accident scene
Emergency aid given for a fee charged to the patient afterward
Reasonable emergency aid given in good faith outside a duty-to-treat setting

explanation: Good Samaritan laws generally shield good-faith emergency helpers acting reasonably; they do not cover intentional misconduct or fraud. Specific protections vary by state.

distractorExplanations.a: Good Samaritan laws protect volunteers without a pre-existing duty; on-duty care is judged by the normal standard of care.
distractorExplanations.b: Gross negligence and willful misconduct are excluded from Good Samaritan protection in virtually every state.
distractorExplanations.c: Charging a fee for the aid generally removes Good Samaritan protection, which covers uncompensated help.

prompt: Which statement about minors and consent is generally true in the U.S.?

options.text: Minors may consent to any care once they turn 16 in every state
A grandparent or school nurse may consent if a parent is not reachable
Emancipated minors still need a parent's signature for routine care
Parents/guardians usually consent for minors, with specific exceptions

explanation: Parental/guardian consent is usual, but state laws create exceptions for emancipated minors and certain sensitive services. Examples of exceptions include certain reproductive and mental health services, which vary by state.

distractorExplanations.a: There is no uniform age-16 rule; the age of majority and minor-consent exceptions vary by state and service.
distractorExplanations.b: Grandparents and school nurses are not default decision-makers without legal guardianship or written authorization.
distractorExplanations.c: Emancipated minors consent to their own care; requiring a parent's signature confuses them with unemancipated minors.

Avoiding actions that may harm the patient during care
